newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's economy continues to boom - economists.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's economy continues to boom - economists.

text.p: Forecasts for Ireland's 1997 economic growth rate will be revised upwards, economists said on Thursday after official figures which confirmed the country's booming economic growth rate in 1996.

"These numbers show that the extent of the boom we have had is unprecedented in Irish economic history. Ireland has had 25 percent growth in three years," Dan McLaughlin, economist with Riada stockbrokers, told Reuters.
Gross domestic product grew by 7.8 percent in 1996 and gross national product was up by 6.9 percent, official figures released by the Central Statistics Office showed.
McLaughlin said he would expect to revise his forecasts for 1997 up to about 7.5 percent, based on the strength of the 1996 outturn.

"If our revised forecasts for 1997 are right at around 7.5 percent GNP growth, then the economy will have expanded by a third in four years, which is absolutely incredible," McLaughlin, Riada's chief economist, said.
Bank of Ireland Group Treasury economist Jim Power said the figures showed there was obviously more momentum in the economy than he anticipated.
"The figures confirm the very strong economy we had last year and which is carrying over into this year," Power said.

"I had forecast GNP of 6.0 percent for 1997. Now I think a growth rate of 6.5 percent should be easily achievable and I expect I will revise 1997 GDP growth up to about 7.0 percent from 6.4 percent," he added.
Analysts forecasts for the 1996 data ranged from 5.8 to 7.9 percent growth for GDP and 4.8 to 8.0 percent for GNP.
Buoyant consumer spending, which rose by 6.3 percent in volume terms over 1995, contributed to the rise in the 1996 aggregates, the CSO said in a statement accompanying the data.
It said there was also a sizeable increase in investment in capital goods, which rose 15.9 percent in volume terms.
Power said he expected the buoyant consumer and investment growth rates to spill over into 1997's performance.

"I think the consumer growth is going to be stronger than I would have anticipated and investment is also likely to be stronger," Power said. "There is obviously more momentum in there than I thought."
McLaughlin said he believed GNP grew by as much as 10 percent in the first quarter of 1997, based on tax revenue and consumer growth data.
"I would say the first quarter (GNP) growth was probably up 10 percent," McLaughlin said.

"If you look at the tax revenue which was averaging growth of 15 percent year-on-year to May and if you look at credit growth that is running at 18-19 percent year-on-year, it all suggests that we have not seen any fall-off in growth."
He said export growth, which saw a slowdown to 10 percent in 1996 from 16.9 percent in 1995, was likely to rise in 1997.
"Given the number of computer companies that have come into Ireland in the last year, I would not be surprised to see exports move back up towards 1995 levels in 1997," he added.
